taj-mahal: A longstanding myth holds that Shah Jahan planned a black-marble mausoleum (the 'Black Taj') across the Yamuna; excavations in the 1990s found only discoloured white stones, not black marble. Nearby, the Mehtab Bagh (Moonlight Garden) on the opposite bank frames the Taj's reflection in its pool, and Agra Fort — where Shah Jahan was imprisoned — stands 2.5 km upstream.
golden-temple: Sikh tradition holds that the site was an ancient amrit kund (pool of nectar): Rama's sons Lava and Kush brought amrit to heal their father, and the excess was poured into the pool, giving Amritsar its name. The Dukh Bhanjani Beri tree on the bank is associated with healing. Nearby, the Jallianwala Bagh memorial lies a short walk from the shrine.
qutub-minar: The minaret's name may honour the Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, whom Iltutmish revered, rather than Qutb-ud-din Aibak. The Iron Pillar in the same courtyard is famous for never rusting — a metallurgical mystery. Nearby, the Mehrauli Archaeological Park holds over 100 monuments spanning 1,000 years.
hampi: The Hampi area is identified with Kishkindha, the monkey kingdom in the Ramayana where Rama met Hanuman and Sugriva. Local tradition holds that Parvati won Shiva through asceticism on Hemakuta Hill, and the Tungabhadra River nearby is called Pampa. Nearby, the Anjaneya Hill (birthplace of Hanuman) and the Sanapur Lake are popular local sites.
charminar: Local tradition holds that Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah prayed for the plague to end and vowed to build a monument where he prayed — the Charminar marks that spot. The Charminar Express train and the Bhagyalakshmi Temple at its base are well-known local landmarks. Nearby, the Laad Bazaar (famous for lac bangles) and Makkah Masjid surround the monument.
rani-ki-vav: Local legend holds that Queen Udayamati built the stepwell as a memorial to her husband King Bhima I, and that a flood of the Saraswati River buried it under silt, which protected its sculptures for centuries until excavation in 1963. Nearby, the Sun Temple at Modhera and the Patan Patola heritage centre are within a short drive.
red-fort: A popular legend holds that the Peacock Throne was encrusted with the Koh-i-Noor diamond, carried off by Nadir Shah in 1739. The Diwan-i-Khas inscription reads: 'If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.' Nearby, Chandni Chowk and Jama Masjid are within walking distance.
humayuns-tomb: Local tradition holds that the tomb's garden was designed by Humayun's wife Bega Begum, who undertook a pilgrimage to Mecca before commissioning it. The tomb is said to have inspired the Taj Mahal's design two generations later. Nearby, the Nizamuddin Dargah and Sunder Nursery are within walking distance.
agra-fort: Legend holds that the fort contains underground passages, some leading to the Taj Mahal. The Musamman Burj, where Shah Jahan was imprisoned, is said to offer the best view of the Taj, and he reportedly spent his final years gazing at it. Nearby, the Itimad-ud-Daulah ('Baby Taj') and Mehtab Bagh are local attractions.
fatehpur-sikri: Local tradition holds that Akbar visited the Sufi saint Salim Chishti at Sikri and was blessed with a son (Jahangir) after the saint's prayers; Akbar then built the city in gratitude. Nearby, the Buland Darwaza (the 'Gate of Victory') and the Dargah of Salim Chishti are the main attractions.
mysore-palace: The palace is said to have been built on the site of an earlier wooden palace that burned down during Dasara in 1897. Legend holds that the new palace blended Hindu, Muslim, Rajput, and Gothic styles, reflecting the Wodeyar dynasty's cosmopolitan outlook. Nearby, Chamundi Hill and the Brindavan Gardens are popular local attractions.
meenakshi: The founding myth holds that King Malayadwaja Pandya prayed for a son but was granted a daughter with three breasts; a voice declared the third would vanish when she met her destined husband. The girl, Meenakshi, met Shiva and her third breast disappeared. Nearby, the Thirumalai Nayakkar Palace and Gandhi Memorial Museum are within walking distance.
ajanta: The caves were rediscovered in 1819 by a British hunting party led by John Smith, who spotted the cave entrance while chasing a tiger. Local shepherds had long known them as 'the seven caves'. Nearby, the Ellora Caves lie about 100 km away and the Bibi Ka Maqbara (the 'Taj of the Deccan') is in Aurangabad.
konark: Legend holds that the temple was built by Samba, son of Krishna, who was cured of leprosy by worshipping Surya here. Another tradition says the 12 wheels represent the 12 months and the 8 spokes the 8 prahars (3-hour periods) of the day. Nearby, Chandrabhaga Beach and the Ramachandi Temple are local attractions.
sanchi: Local tradition holds that Ashoka chose the site because of its proximity to Vidisha, where his wife Devi was born. The stupa was built to enshrine the relics of the Buddha. Nearby, the Udayagiri Caves (with Gupta-era rock-cut sculptures) and the Heliodorus Pillar at Vidisha are within a short drive.
khajuraho: Local tradition attributes the temples to King Chandravarman, born to Hemvati after she was seduced by the moon god Chandra; the temples were built to wash away the sin of this union. Nearby, the Panna Tiger Reserve and the Raneh Falls (a canyon of crystalline granite) are popular local attractions.
jantar-mantar: Jai Singh II is said to have built the instruments so large because he believed larger masonry instruments would be more accurate than small brass ones. The Samrat Yantra's shadow moves at about 1 mm per second. Nearby, the City Palace and Hawa Mahal are within walking distance.
ellora: Local legend holds that the Kailasa temple was built by a queen who vowed to fast until the temple's shikhara was visible; to speed construction, the architect carved downward from the top of the rock instead of building up. Nearby, the Grishneshwar Temple (one of the 12 Jyotirlingas) and Daulatabad Fort are local attractions.
mahabalipuram: Local tradition holds that the temple was part of a group of seven pagodas, of which six are submerged. European sailors mentioned the 'Seven Pagodas' myth, and a 2004 tsunami briefly exposed submerged structures offshore. Nearby, Arjuna's Penance and the Five Rathas are within walking distance.
brihadeeswarar: Local legend holds that the 80-tonne capstone of the vimana was rolled up a 6.5 km ramp. The temple's shadow is said to never fall on the ground at noon — a claim debunked but persistent in local tradition. Nearby, the Thanjavur Maratha Palace and the Saraswathi Mahal Library are local attractions.
champaner: Local tradition holds that the city was named after a Bhil chieftain named Champa, defeated by the Solanki king. The site's Jain temples and mosques stand side by side, reflecting the pluralistic culture of the Gujarat Sultanate. Nearby, the Kalika Mata Temple on Pavagadh Hill is a major pilgrimage site.
gateway-india: A popular legend holds that the Gateway was built to commemorate King George V's 1911 visit, but the arch was not completed until 1924. The last British troops to leave India in 1948 passed through it in a ceremonial march. Nearby, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel and the Elephanta Caves ferry are local attractions.
mahabodhi: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under a Bodhi tree at this spot. The current tree is said to be a descendant of the original, propagated from a cutting taken to Sri Lanka by Sanghamitta. Nearby, the Thai Temple and the Great Buddha Statue (80 ft) are local attractions.
bhimbetka: Local tradition associates the rock shelters with Bhima, the Pandava hero of the Mahabharata, who is said to have rested here during his exile. The shelters contain some of India's oldest rock paintings, dating to the Upper Paleolithic. Nearby, the Bhojpur Temple (with its massive Shiva lingam) is a local attraction.
kamakhya: According to the Kalika Purana, the temple marks the spot where Sati's yoni fell when Shiva carried her body. The temple is said to have been destroyed and rebuilt multiple times; the current structure dates to the 17th century. Nearby, the Umananda Temple (on Peacock Island in the Brahmaputra) is a local attraction.
